extracted.intended_audience: NLP researchers and developers working on satire/humor detection, computational deception detection, and automated fake-news filtering
extracted.subtask_description: Identify whether a news-style article is satirical or legitimate by extracting linguistic, semantic, and discourse-level cues and applying machine-learning classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absurdity
rubrics_metrics.description: Defined by the unexpected introduction of new named entities (people, places, locations) within the final sentence of satirical news; the article is deemed absurd when the set of named entities present in the last line does not intersect with those appearing in the rest of the article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implemented with NLTK POS tagging and Named Entity Recognition; treat Absurdity as a binary feature (0=non-absurd, 1=absurd). Example: final line introducing previously unseen entities (e.g., 'Christopher Hitchens Memorial University') signals absurdity; motivated by the semantic-validity notion from Burfoot & Baldwin (2009).

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor (punchline / opposing scripts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Captures the presence of a punchline/opposing scripts by measuring semantic relatedness between the lead (first) sentence and the final (last) sentence — satirical articles often have minimal relatedness between these two segments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign binary humor feature when relatedness(first_sentence, last_sentence) is minimal relative to other sentences. Compute relatedness via a knowledge-based word-to-word metric (Wu & Palmer 1994) aggregated over segments. Intended to operationalize punchline detection / incongruity resolution; example: final line that is semantically dissimilar from setup indicates humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grammar (LIWC / parts-of-speech profile)
rubrics_metrics.description: Normalized term frequencies of grammatical categories (adjectives, adverbs, pronouns, conjunctions, prepositions) using LIWC dictionaries to capture syntactic and stylistic differences between satirical and legitimate news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use LIWC2015 category counts or POS-tag-derived counts as a feature vector. Grammar feature also encodes sentence complexity tendencies (e.g., more dependent clauses in quotations). Guidance: normalize by article length.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: Normalized frequencies of punctuation marks (periods, commas, colon, semi-colon, question marks, exclamation points, quotes) as satirical articles tend to use more punctuation due to longer/clause-heavy sentences and comedic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Count punctuation occurrences and normalize by article length. High counts (especially more commas and clause punctuation) can be predictive of satire; this feature improved precision in experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative Affect (polarity / emotional scenarios)
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence and normalized frequency of negative-affect terms (words conveying negative emotions) as measured by sentiment/dictionary resources (e.g., LIWC).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include as a normalized feature weight. The paper found that negative affect improved classification performance; positive polarity signals did not show similar improvement in their trials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Baseline tf*idf topic vector
rubrics_metrics.description: Topic-based document representation using term frequency–inverse document frequency weighting on tokenized unigrams and bigrams (with stopword removal and normalization by article length) as a baseline classifier feature set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tf*idf vectors (normalized by article length) with a linear SVM as baseline. In this study the tf*idf baseline achieved ~82% accuracy (F-score=82%).

rubrics_metrics.name: Word-level lexical cues (headlines, n-grams, counterfactual & temporal words, profanity/slang)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lexical and semantic word-level signals such as headline style, profanity/slang, counterfactual words (e.g., 'nevertheless', 'yet'), temporal-compression words ('now', 'abruptly'), and n-gram patterns that correlate with satire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extract unigrams/bigrams and lexical markers; prior work shows tf*idf on bi-grams as a useful baseline; profanity/slang were important in some corpora but did not add predictive power in this dataset. Headlines themselves are especially relevant: satire often repeats or extends headline material in first line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semantic validity / named-entity co-occurrence (Burfoot & Baldwin-style)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure of imbalances in co-occurring named entities — legitimate news tends to show consistent co-occurrence patterns of entities, while satire introduces semantically disparate or unlikely entity combinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute entity co-occurrence statistics across a corpus and flag low-cooccurrence or semantically disparate entity combinations as indicators of absurdity; can be operationalized by comparing entity co-occurrence profiles or using semantic distance in a knowledge graph.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentence complexity / run-on sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Syntactic complexity features such as sentence length, number of clauses, and density of dependent clauses, especially in quotations; satirical articles often pack more clauses for comedic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure clause counts, punctuation density, parse-based complexity metrics. Note: in this study simple words-per-sentence did not increase predictive accuracy, but clause-level complexity and punctuation did. Use grammatical parse or regex patterns to detect run-on or clause-heavy constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semantic relatedness metrics (WordNet / Wu & Palmer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge-based similarity measures (e.g., Wu & Palmer 1994 using WordNet) to compute word-to-word and segment-to-segment relatedness, used to detect incongruity between segments (setup vs. punchline).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For two segments S1 and S2, for each word in S1 find most related word in S2 (and vice versa), weight/sum and normalize by lengths; average the two directions. Lower relatedness between lead and final sentence indicates possible satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sarcasm / irony surface markers
rubrics_metrics.description: Surface-level markers associated with sarcasm and irony such as atypical punctuation, frequent specific words, title/metadata quirks, and explicit lexical cues that signal saying the opposite of the literal meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use features like punctuation patterns, exclamation/question marks, hyperbolic phrasing, and lexical indicators; combine with context/world-knowledge heuristics where possible. Prior work found models using such features achieved reasonable precision/recall for sarcasm detection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline and final-line salience (structural discourse cues)
rubrics_metrics.description: The headline and final line are especially informative: legitimate news typically reports new material in the first line (inverted pyramid), while satire often repeats the title in first line and uses the final line as a punchline/non-sequitur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extract and compare headline → lead → final sentence relations (semantic overlap/distance); detect final-line non sequiturs or introduction of new entities/concepts. These structural cues were repeatedly observed and informed Absurdity/Humor features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dataset construction: matched satirical-legitimate article pairing
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect satirical and legitimate articles in matched pairs by country, topic, and domain (e.g., 2x2x4x3 design) to control topicality and provenance in experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For robust evaluation, match each satirical article with a legitimate article published in the same country and similar subject matter. Reserve portions of the combined dataset for training/testing and use cross-validation for reliability; e.g., 75% training / 25% holdout with 10-fold CV on training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Processing & modeling hygiene (normalization, tokenization, feature weighting, SVM/CV)
rubrics_metrics.description: Operational requirements for building the classifier: stopword removal, tokenization into unigrams/bigrams, tf*idf weighting normalized by article length, use of linear SVM for binary classification, and evaluation via 10-fold cross-validation plus holdout testing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow pipeline: preprocess → tokenize → tf*idf (length-normalized) → feature augmentation (Abs, Hum, Gram, Neg, Pun) → train linear SVM → evaluate with cross-validation and held-out test set. This procedural rubric ensures reproducible and comparable performance reporting.
